newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Diana takes her anti-mine crusade to Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Diana takes her anti-mine crusade to Bosnia.

text.p: Britain's Princess Diana took her crusade against landmines on Friday to Bosnia, a country still recovering from a devastating war.

The princess paid her first visit to a Bosnian mine victim in the northeastern town of Tuzla, where she spoke for 45 minutes with Franjo Kresic, a former soldier who lost his leg in a mine blast during the country's 1992-95 war.
Diana emerged from the rundown apartment block smiling and waving at neighborhood children who gathered to greet her.
Diana, looking deeply tanned and fit, beamed as she patted the children on the head and shook their hands as they chanted "Diana! Diana!"

She gave a cold stare to reporters when they asked her to confirm British newspaper accounts linking her to film producer Dodi Fayed, son of Egyptian tycoon Mohammed Al-Fayed, who owns London luxury department store Harrods.
The divorced princess, trying to forge a role as a roving humanitarian ambassador, planned to highlight the suffering caused by mines in a three-day "private visit" to Bosnia.

Diana's white private Lear jet touched down earlier on Friday as a gaggle of press waited on the tarmac of Sarajevo airport, once the scene of vicious fighting between rival armies during the Bosnian conflict.
Dressed in a pale blue shirt, blue blazer, cropped blue jeans and suede flat pumps, Diana shook hands with British Ambassador Charles Crawford and climbed into a van headed for Tuzla.

On the morning of her departure, British tabloids were full of speculation about Diana's friendship with 41-year old Fayed and said she had been seen entering his luxury London apartment for a dinner date.
The Daily Mail's front page headline read: "Diana -- it's a real romance", while The Sun said: "Romantic meal in new love's London flat -- then farewell kiss before Bosnia".
Her 15-year marriage to British royal heir Prince Charles ended in divorce last year.
Diana, 36, was invited to Sarajevo by the Washington-based Landmine Survivors' Network, which tries to raise funds for mine victims and to promote a ban on the weapons.

It is the second time Diana has visited a former war zone on her anti-mine campaign. The first trip, to Angola in January, brought home to many around the world the terrible toll inflicted on civilians by the millions of anti-personnel mines left behind by war.

Diana was not expected to visit Serb-controlled territory in Bosnia, where anti-British feeling is running high following an operation by British special forces to arrest two Serbs wanted for war crimes which resulted in one of them being shot dead.
Her support for a worldwide ban on anti-personnel mines irritated the previous Conservative government but the new Labour Foreign Secretary Robin Cook endorsed her Bosnia visit.
Whatever the merits of her campaign, Britain's royalty-obsessed tabloid newspapers were preoccupied with her new romance with Dodi.
"Princess Diana has embarked on her first serious romance since she and Charles divorced," the Daily Mail's royal correspondent Richard Kay said.
Newspapers printed pictures of Diana on a boat enjoying a summer holiday in the Mediterranean with Dodi, a film producer who has dated Hollywood starlets.
Diana was said to be so "relaxed" about the affair becoming public knowledge that she was "unconcerned" at the prospect of intimate photographs of the couple being published.
The new pictures, said to show the couple kissing, have been the subject of a bidding war among newspapers and magazines in Europe.
